name: Narikala Fortress
label: Narikala Fortress
camera_source: Commons cluster (49 photos). Moved 63 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 30 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9820020: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Narikala' (200 m across).
notes: Ancient hilltop fortress with sweeping views over the old town.

text.description:
Narikala is an old hilltop fortress above Tbilisi, looking down on the Mtkvari (Kura) River. It stands on a steep hill between the sulphur baths and the botanical gardens, and it has two walled sections. Most of the stonework you see today dates from the 16th and 17th centuries, though a fortress has stood here since about the year 364. Parts were damaged by an earthquake in 1827 and later pulled down. In the lower court is the church of St Nicholas, built in 1996-1997 to replace a 13th-century church lost to fire.

It photographs well because the weathered walls give you strong foreground shapes, with the city and river spread out behind them. A single wall or tower with open sky above it makes a simple, clear picture, and a wider shot of the walls climbing the slope shows the scale of the place.

For a phone, start with the default lens (1x) and use gridlines to keep the walls straight. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of masonry, and use the telephoto or zoom for details such as the church or a single tower. Take a few steps between shots, as the view changes quickly on this slope.
text.geographic_location: Narikala sits on a steep hill above the old part of Tbilisi, between the sulphur baths and the botanical gardens, overlooking the Mtkvari (Kura) River.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot. The fortress lies on a steep hill between the sulphur baths and the botanical gardens. Once the middle of the fortress is about 1 minute on foot to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the walls and the church. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole sweep of fortifications, and the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for towers and rooftops in the city below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Metekhi Bridge (middle of the bridge, looking upstream toward the fortress). Narikala rising over the Old Town rooftops and the river, with Metekhi Church in the foreground. From here the main body of the walls lies to the south-west, so face that way for your main shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a wall or tower up with one of them so the stonework stays straight. Keep some sky above the walls, and for a wider shot use the ultra-wide (0.5x) with the near wall low in the frame. Stay clear of the edges of walls and steep drops when stepping back.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. If you want a wide view along the walls, try panorama and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset, when the light is softer and the stone looks warmer. Midday sun can make the sky look washed out.

text.access_note: This is a historic fortress site on a hillside, so check the official site before you go for access details.

name: Metekhi Church
label: Metekhi Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Metekhi Church' (5 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1064270003: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Metekhi Church' (31 m across).
notes: Church on a cliff above the Kura with the King Vakhtang Gorgasali statue.

text.description:
Metekhi Church stands right on the edge of a cliff above the Kura river, looking across to the Old Town. It was built to look like a continuation of the rock beneath it, and that is why it shows up so clearly in city views. The church you see today mostly dates from between 1278 and 1289, in the reign of King Demetrius II. Oral tradition traces the site back to the 5th century, though there is no firm evidence for that. The building is small, about 20 by 16 metres, and slightly tall for its footprint. Its history is a varied one: a prison in the Russian Empire period, a store for museum collections, and a youth theatre in the 1970s.

The churchyard terrace next to the King Vakhtang Gorgasali statue is the classic free photo spot. From the cliff edge you look down over the Old Town rooftops, the river and the domed sulphur baths, with the statue as a strong foreground. Remember that the courtyard views are mostly of the city rather than of the church itself. For a shot of the church on its cliff, use Metekhi Bridge, where the Old Town and Narikala Fortress rise behind it, or the Bridge of Peace. On the terrace, keep the statue on one side of the frame and let the river and rooftops fill the rest. Late afternoon gives warm light, and early morning is quieter.
text.geographic_location: Metekhi Church is in Tbilisi on the Metekhi Cliff, on the left bank of the Kura (Mtkvari) river. It faces the Old Town from across the water.
text.directions_text: From the Old Town, the church is directly across the river on the cliff, next to the King Vakhtang Gorgasali statue. Metekhi Bridge crosses the river just below the church. No public-transport stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach the church. The phone icon on the map marks the church itself. For the view, walk to the churchyard terrace beside the statue. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the terrace view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the statue and the rooftops in one frame. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the domed sulphur baths or the Old Town roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the view, walk to the churchyard terrace on the cliff edge beside the King Vakhtang Gorgasali statue. From the terrace the photo shows the Old Town rooftops, the river, the domed sulphur baths and the horse-and-rider statue. The church itself is best photographed from Metekhi Bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the statue on one third of the frame, with the river and rooftops filling the rest. Hold the phone low and close to the statue for a stronger foreground. For a picture of the church itself, walk to Metekhi Bridge, where the church sits in front of the Old Town and Narikala Fortress. The Bridge of Peace also gives a framed view, but check the angle when you get there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rooftops to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Wind can shake the phone on the exposed terrace, so hold it with both hands and take a couple of frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset for warm light. Early morning is quieter.

text.access_note: The terrace is open-air and free, but the church is a place of worship: dress modestly (shoulders and knees covered, head covering for women), avoid flash, and ask before photographing worshippers. Visiting times vary, so check locally before you go.

name: Freedom Square, Tbilisi
label: Freedom Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Shota Rustaveli Avenue' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Shota Rustaveli Avenue nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/709370328: 'Freedom Monument', the best-known feature inside 'Freedom Square' (237 m across).
notes: Central square with the golden St George column.

text.description: Freedom Square sits at the eastern end of Rustaveli Avenue, the main street of Tbilisi, and the gilded figure of St George slaying the dragon stands in the middle of it. For a second view, walk to Rustaveli Avenue and look east, where the square and the St George column are framed at the end of a tree-lined street, so you see the monument as the city's main street leads to it. The monument is a recent arrival. A large statue of Lenin stood here from 1956 until it was symbolically pulled down in August 1991. The St George monument by Zurab Tsereteli was unveiled in the same place on 23 November 2006. The place was first called Freedom Square in 1918, and six streets branch out from it, including Rustaveli Avenue and Pushkin Street. The square is a busy roundabout, so take your photos from the pavements and keep your phone and bag close, as guides warn about pickpockets. Look for a clear gap between passers-by and keep the column in the centre of the frame. If you shoot from the avenue, let the line of trees lead the eye towards it. If you want a quieter, higher view, the top of the monument appears level with the old city's rooftops from the Betlemi Street stairs. Confirm the exact steps on the map once you are there.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Tbilisi, Georgia, at the eastern end of Rustaveli Avenue. The Tbilisi City Assembly and the Courtyard by Marriott Tbilisi are among the buildings on the square.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Tbilisi and head for Freedom Square at the eastern end of Rustaveli Avenue. If you would rather take the avenue view, stop on Rustaveli Avenue where the column is framed by the trees. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the monument in its setting. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the buildings and trees, but keep the column away from the edges, where it can look stretched. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the monument.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Shota Rustaveli Avenue (looking back east along the avenue toward the square). The square and the St. George column framed at the end of the tree-lined avenue, with the square seen from the avenue's length. From there you look south-west towards the St George column.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the column on the central vertical line. If you are on the avenue, let the trees run down both sides to lead the eye. Wait for a gap in the traffic and passers-by. For a different angle, the Betlemi Street stairs show the top of the monument level with the old city's rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the column to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the gold doesn't wash out against the sky. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the column is lit, is the most striking time. Early morning is likely to be quieter for clear views along the avenue.

text.access_note: Freedom Square is an open public space, but it may be closed or crowded during state events, so check on the day before you go.

name: Mtatsminda Park
label: Mtatsminda Park
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/13443464: large area 'Mtatsminda Park' (1182 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Hilltop amusement park reached by funicular, with a panoramic city view.

text.description: Mtatsminda Park is a landscaped hilltop park above Tbilisi, with carousels, a roller-coaster, a dark ride and a big Ferris wheel set at the edge of the mountain. It photographs well because you get the fairground and the city in one view. The park sits about 770 metres up, the highest point in Tbilisi, and covers more than 100 hectares, so there is plenty of room to move around and try different angles. The Giant Wheel is the tallest ride, at 65 metres, and takes 10 to 12 minutes for one turn. That makes it a handy foreground shape, or a way to add a bit of colour to a city view. The park can be reached by funicular, which opened in 1905 and links Chonkadze Street with the park. The carriages and the old railway are a nice subject on their own. The park was founded in the 1930s, in the Soviet period. Use the wheel and the rides as a frame for the rooftops below, and keep the horizon level using your phone's gridlines. If the city looks hazy, move closer to the rides and shoot the shapes and colours instead. Take a few frames from the same spot at different zoom levels, so you have both a wide scene and a tighter detail to choose from.
text.geographic_location: At the top of Mount Mtatsminda, overlooking Tbilisi. The park looks out over the city from the highest point in the capital.
text.directions_text: From Chonkadze Street in central Tbilisi you can take the funicular up to the park; check the official site before you go for running times. The park is also connected to a motorway. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the rides and the view together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole wheel and the city in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out rooftops and details far below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mtatsminda View Point (large viewing deck along the front of the Restaurant Funicular building, facing the city). A wide panorama of Tbilisi's rooftops, the river and landmarks such as Sameba Cathedral and Narikala Fortress, with Mtatsminda's slope and the park behind the viewer. Step a few paces either way to keep fairground structures from blocking the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Use the Giant Wheel or a ride as a strong shape on one side, and leave the city view on the other. Keep your phone level, as tall structures look odd when tilted. For people shots, use portrait mode with the rides soft behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the city or the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the lights do not blow out. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against a rail or your body to stay steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into evening, when the light is softer and the city lights start to come on. Midday is fine for bright colourful ride shots, but the distant view can look flat.

text.access_note: This is a theme park on a hilltop, so access to the park and rides may involve tickets or restrictions; check the official site before you go.

name: Holy Trinity Cathedral of Tbilisi
label: Sameba Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Betlemi Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Betlemi Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/585352693: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Holy Trinity Cathedral of Tbilisi' (95 m across).
notes: Huge golden-domed cathedral on Elia Hill.

text.description: Sameba, as locals call it, is the main cathedral of the Georgian Orthodox Church and one of the biggest churches in the Orthodox world. It was built between 1995 and 2004 on Elia Hill in Avlabari, on the left bank of the Kura, and it is the third-tallest Eastern Orthodox cathedral anywhere. From the base to the top of its gilded cross it stands 86.1 metres, and the cross alone is 7.5 metres. That height is why it photographs so well. It rises above the older city and is easy to pick out from a long way off. The Old Town side offers a more characterful picture than a straight-on shot. On Betlemi Street, a stretch with a restaurant balcony lets you use the balcony as a foreground frame, with the gilt dome sitting behind it. This is a separate viewpoint from the map's stand-here point. It is described as less crowded than the fortress viewpoint. The cathedral was designed by Archil Mindiashvili and consecrated on 23 November 2004. Its style is a modern take on traditional Georgian church building, with extra vertical emphasis. For your phone, if you use the balcony view, keep the balcony and the dome both in the picture rather than zooming in too tightly. Then take a second, closer shot of the dome and cross. If you have time, the cathedral grounds give a different view, with the facade and dome rising straight up and the city behind. Narikala Fortress is a third option, showing the golden dome above the dense city.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands on Elia Hill in the Avlabari neighbourhood of Old Tbilisi, on the left bank of the Kura (Mtkvari) river. The Betlemi Street balcony view is a separate viewpoint on the Old Town side.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Old Town. If you want that framing, look on Betlemi Street for the stretch with the restaurant balcony and look up toward the cathedral. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the balcony and the dome in one frame if you are at the Betlemi Street balcony view. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the dome and cross. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are in the cathedral grounds and want the full facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Betlemi Street (stretch with the restaurant balcony, looking up toward the cathedral). The gilt dome of the cathedral framed by a restaurant balcony in the foreground, from the Old Town side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the dome on one of the upper intersections. At the Betlemi Street viewpoint, let the balcony fill the lower or side edge as a frame. Hold the phone level so the cathedral does not lean. For a second shot, step in for a close telephoto of the dome and cross. If you want a different angle, the cathedral grounds show the facade and dome rising straight up, and Narikala Fortress shows the dome above the city with the river beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the gilt does not glare and the sky stays blue. Take a few frames in case people walk into the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or evening. One guide advises against midday because the light is glary.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is on a public street, but the cathedral is a place of worship: photography is generally allowed outside and in the grounds, but restricted inside the main nave, especially during services, and flash should be avoided. Check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Modest dress is customary when visiting an Orthodox cathedral.
Midday light on the gilded dome can be glary, so lowering the exposure slider helps.
The exact balcony may change.

name: Kartlis Deda
label: Mother of Georgia
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kartlis Deda' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1063062536: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Mother of Kartli' (9 m across).
notes: Aluminium statue of a woman with a sword and a wine cup above the city.

text.description:
Kartlis Deda, the Mother of Kartli, is a 20-metre aluminium figure of a woman in Georgian national dress. She stands on top of Sololaki hill and looks out over Tbilisi. She is a good subject because she stands high above the Old Town, so a photo can show the statue and the city together. The monument was put up in 1958, when Tbilisi celebrated its 1500th anniversary, and was designed by the sculptor Elguja Amashukeli. In her left hand she holds a bowl of wine for friends, and in her right hand a sword for enemies, so these two details are worth a close-up. The statue you see today replaced the earlier one in 1997.

Guides say the figure is too tall to photograph well from right under her feet. Take your first photos from the viewing platform at her feet, then walk a few steps back so the whole figure fits in with the Old Town and the skyline behind her. Space in front of the statue is limited, and the top can get crowded, so be patient and shoot when people move away. If you want a different view, Metekhi Church shows the statue on the ridge above the Old Town rooftops. The National Botanical Garden of Georgia shows her from the wooded slope below, with the Kura River valley.
text.geographic_location: Kartlis Deda stands on top of Sololaki hill, on the ridge above Tbilisi's Old Town. Narikala Fortress is nearby, and the Kura River runs through the valley below.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground or tram stop at this spot, so start from Rike Park, below the ridge, and take the cable car up. You can also walk up on foot along the Narikala trail. The statue is at the top of the ridge, so allow extra time for the climb. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the platform to get the statue and the skyline in one frame. Back at the default lens (1x), a few steps away, the figure looks more natural. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the wine bowl, the sword and the rooftops below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take a few photos from there. Then step back a little so the whole figure and the Old Town skyline fit in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the statue upright. Use them to place her on one side and let the city fill the other. Hold the phone level, because tilting it upwards from close by makes the figure look squashed. If you want another view, try Metekhi Church for the statue above the Old Town rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. Take a few shots in a row, because people often walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon around golden hour, or early morning, as guides suggest. These are the calmer, softer-light times of day.

text.access_note: The statue is on an open hilltop reached by the Rike Park cable car or on foot; check the official site before you go for cable car details.

name: Abanotubani
label: Sulfur Baths
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2073134: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Abanotubani' (468 m across).
notes: Historic bath district with domed brick roofs.

text.description:
Abanotubani (literally 'bath district') is the old district of Tbilisi, known for its sulphur baths. It sits on the eastern bank of the Mtkvari River, at the foot of Narikala fortress. Local legend says King Vakhtang Gorgasali of Iberia's falcon fell, which led to the discovery of the hot springs. The king found the warm water and decided to found a new capital on the spot. By the end of the 13th century the city had 65 baths, so bathing has shaped this corner of town for a very long time.

It photographs well because so much is packed into a small area. You get the bathhouse roofs, narrow lanes, old balconies and the fortress hill rising behind. It works as a general scene of old Tbilisi rather than a single building, so take a few frames instead of hunting for one perfect angle. Start with a wide shot to show how the roofs sit below the hillside. Then move closer for details such as doorways, brickwork and street corners. The district is compact, so you can cover it slowly on foot, and the whole area is only a short walk across from the phone icon on the map. Keep an eye on passing people and traffic in narrow spots, and step aside before you stop to shoot.
text.geographic_location: Abanotubani is in the old part of Tbilisi, on the east bank of the Mtkvari River at the foot of Narikala fortress. It lies across the water from the Metekhisubani area.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the old town below Narikala fortress and look for the sulphur baths. Then follow the map to the phone icon on the map. From there the middle of the bath district is about 72 m to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m north-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the roofs, lane and hillside together, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as rooflines and doorways.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Stop wherever the lane opens up enough to show the roofs with the hillside behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of buildings straight, especially with the ultra-wide, which can make walls lean. Include a strip of the fortress hill above the roofs to show where you are. Take one wide scene and two or three close detail shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white and the building colours stay rich. Wipe the lens first, as steam or damp air can leave a haze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the lanes. Evening is good for warm street light, and night mode can help once it gets dark.

text.access_note: The streets are part of the city, but individual bathhouses are businesses, so check the official site of any bath before you go.

name: Bridge of Peace
label: Bridge of Peace
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 78 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 70 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1207561125: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bridge of Peace' (149 m across).
notes: Glass and steel pedestrian bridge over the Kura river.

text.description: The Bridge of Peace is a curved pedestrian bridge of steel and glass across the Kura River in central Tbilisi. It links Rike Park with the Old Town. It opened on 6 May 2010 and is about 150 metres long. The Italian architect Michele De Lucchi designed it, and the sweeping canopy looks a little like a sea creature. That shape is the reason it photographs well. The curve gives you a strong line to lead the eye, and the glass catches light and reflections. After dark the canopy carries 1,208 LED fixtures that run through four lighting programmes. One of them makes the roof twinkle like stars. Lights in the glass railings also switch on as people walk past. Behind the bridge you can pick out Metekhi Church, the statue of Vakhtang Gorgasali and Narikala Fortress on one side, and Baratashvili Bridge and the Ceremonial Palace on the other. Not everyone likes it, because some critics thought a modern structure was out of place beside the old town, so it is a good place to show old and new in one frame. On the bridge itself, walkers will often be in your shot, so be patient or use them to show scale. Take a few frames across a full hour if you can, as the light patterns change.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the Kura River in central Tbilisi, between Rike Park on one bank and the Old Town on the other. Metekhi Church and Narikala Fortress are visible from the bridge.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop listed for this spot, so walk to Rike Park or the bridge from central Tbilisi. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole curve of the canopy into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view along the walkway. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull in Narikala Fortress or Metekhi Church behind the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Baratashvili Bridge. A front-on view of the Bridge of Peace with the Old Town buildings rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the line of the walkway on one of them so the curve leads into the picture. Keep the horizon level, because the canopy makes a crooked frame obvious. Try one wide shot with the full bridge, then a tighter 2x-5x shot of the Old Town behind it. For a bit of movement, try a Live Photo or short motion clip as the light patterns change.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, let night mode do its work and hold the phone against a railing or your elbows tucked in, to keep it still. Tap the brightest part of the canopy to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the LEDs keep their detail and do not wash out into white blobs.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go after dark, when the lights are on: they run from 90 minutes before sunset until 90 minutes after sunrise. Stay for a while, as the canopy changes its pattern every hour. The short period just after sunset, when the sky still has some colour, is a good moment.

text.access_note: It is an open pedestrian bridge in the city, but check the official site before you go in case of any works or closures.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point is on the Rike Park (east bank) end of the bridge, so the view from it looks west towards the Old Town.
The short period just after sunset, when the sky still has some colour, gives a good balance between sky and bridge lights.
Pedestrians on the bridge may appear in photos, particularly in the evening.

name: Rustaveli Avenue
label: Rustaveli Avenue
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mtatsminda Park' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Mtatsminda Park Map' (pois).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Main boulevard lined with grand 19th-century buildings.

text.description:
Rustaveli Avenue is the main street of central Tbilisi. It starts at Freedom Square and runs for about 1.5 km, lined with the Parliament, the Opera Theatre, the Rustaveli Theatre, Kashveti Church and several museums. It was laid out in the 1840s on the orders of the Russian viceroy Mikhail Vorontsov, who wanted to give a Persian-style city a more European feel. It took its present name, after the medieval poet Shota Rustaveli, in 1918.

On this map the photo is taken from Mtatsminda Park, the hilltop park above the avenue. From up here you get a wide view of the whole city, and in the evening Rustaveli Street shows up as a line among the lights below. That makes it a good second stop after you have walked the avenue itself. The cable car to the hill leaves from behind the Academy of Sciences. It opened in 1959, closed in 1990 and reopened in October 2024.

The cable car is a paid ride, so check current operation before you go. If you would rather see the avenue at street level, Freedom Square is a good alternative. From there the whole avenue runs away from you, framed by plane trees, buses and stone apartment blocks, with the St George column close by. Works on the avenue were due to close it to traffic until the end of 2026, so parts may be fenced off.
text.geographic_location: Rustaveli Avenue is in the centre of Tbilisi and runs from Freedom Square for about 1.5 km. Mtatsminda hill and its park rise above it.
text.directions_text: Start on Rustaveli Avenue near the Academy of Sciences, where the cable car to Mtatsminda Park leaves from behind the building. Check that it is running before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the city and the glow of the avenue. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the line of Rustaveli Street among the lights. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole hillside and skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Mtatsminda Park (hilltop park above the avenue, reached by the cable car from behind the Academy of Sciences). A wide evening view of the city from the hill, with Rustaveli Street visible among the lights below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the line of the avenue on one of the lower grid lines, leaving the sky or the far hills above. If you prefer street level, Freedom Square is the other good spot. Stand at the start of the avenue and shoot straight down its length, with the plane trees on both sides.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, switch on night mode and brace your elbows on a wall or railing to keep still. Tap on the brightest part of the city to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights don't burn out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: In the evening, after dark, when the avenue shows up among the city lights.

text.access_note: Mtatsminda Park is an open public park, but the cable car up is a paid ride, so check the official site for current operation before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Telephoto (2x-5x) helps pick out the line of the avenue from the hilltop.
Leaning on a wall or railing helps keep a night-mode shot steady.
Lowering the exposure slider helps stop bright city lights burning out in night shots.

name: Anchiskhati Basilica
label: Anchiskhati Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ioane Shavteli Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Ioane Shavteli Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/337365208: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Anchiskhati Basilica of Saint Mary' (27 m across).
notes: Oldest surviving church in Tbilisi, near Shardeni Street.

text.description:
Anchiskhati is the oldest surviving church in Tbilisi, and it sits in a tangle of narrow old streets, so the photos are about brick, carved stone and small details rather than one big sweeping view. The Georgian annals credit King Dachi of Iberia, who ruled around 522-534, with building it. The church took the name Anchiskhati in 1675, when a treasured icon of the Saviour was brought to Tbilisi to keep it safe from an Ottoman invasion. The brick belfry beside it dates from the same year. In the 1950s and 60s a restoration brought the church back to its seventeenth-century look, which is why you see so much brick today.

The best frame is the eastern side, as you walk along Ioane Shavteli Street. From there you can take in the relief of the Exaltation of the Cross and the brick bell tower in one photo, with the street itself leading the eye towards them. If you have time, step into the courtyard gateway as well. The arched brick entrance, its crucifix and the metal arbour with vines make a quieter, closer picture than the facade. Photography inside is officially prohibited, though guides report mixed practice, so stick to exterior views. This is a working church, so be discreet and quiet.
text.geographic_location: Anchiskhati Basilica stands in the old town of Tbilisi, on Ioane Shavteli Street among narrow, uneven lanes. The photo spot is on that street, just south of the church.
text.directions_text: From central Tbilisi, head to the old town, then continue on foot to Ioane Shavteli Street. The lanes are narrow and uneven, so watch your step while looking at your screen. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the eastern facade and the street. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Exaltation of the Cross relief and the top of the bell tower. In the courtyard gateway, the ultra-wide (0.5x) can help in the tight space, but keep the arch straight so the lines do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ioane Shavteli Street (eastern facade, approaching along the street). The eastern facade with its Exaltation of the Cross relief and the brick bell tower, framed by the street. Stay to the side of the street so people and vehicles can pass.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the street's edges as lines leading to the church, keeping the bell tower upright. Take one wider shot with the street, then one closer shot of the relief and tower. For a quieter alternative, photograph the arched brick gateway with its crucifix and the metal arbour from the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall or the relief to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the brick keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands, since narrow streets are often shaded and your phone may slow its shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when warm light falls on the western face of the bell tower, according to one guide. On the day, check where the shade falls on the eastern facade before you settle on a shot.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street, but the church is an active place of worship where photography inside is officially prohibited, though guides report mixed practice, and women are expected to cover their heads, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Anchiskhati Basilica is in the old town of Tbilisi, on or near Ioane Shavteli Street.
The exterior can be photographed from the public street without a ticket.
In late afternoon the eastern facade may be in shade or flatter light, because the warm light that guides mention falls on the western face of the bell tower.
Narrow, shaded lanes can make a phone use a slower shutter speed.

name: Tbilisi Sioni Cathedral
label: Sioni Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sioni Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Sioni Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/77895547: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sioni Cathedral of the Dormition' (51 m across).
notes: Medieval cathedral in the old town.

text.description: Sioni Cathedral is a working Georgian Orthodox church on Sioni Street, in the old part of central Tbilisi. Its eastern side faces the right bank of the Kura River. It photographs well because the pale yellow stone walls, the plain, sturdy shapes and the separate bell tower sit among the Old Town rooftops, so you get a good sense of place in one frame. The church takes its name from Mount Zion in Jerusalem and has been rebuilt many times since the 6th and 7th centuries. The building you see today is based on a 13th-century version, with changes made between the 17th and 19th centuries. Its stone comes from Bolnisi, a town to the south-west of Tbilisi. It was the main Georgian Orthodox cathedral until the Holy Trinity Cathedral was consecrated in 2004. The three-storey bell tower stands in the courtyard to the north. It dates from a rebuilding in 1425, was largely destroyed in 1795 and was restored in 1939. A separate, approximate alternative is the lane to the south of the church, which may show the bell tower against the Old Town roofline. The exact spot there is approximate, so walk a few steps either way until the tower sits cleanly above the roofs. A further option is the courtyard, where the bell tower makes a strong focal point for shots of the church. Please be discreet around worshippers and avoid photographing them.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town of central Tbilisi, on Sioni Street, a short walk from the right bank of the Kura River, which the cathedral's eastern side faces.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Old Town on the right bank of the Kura River and look for Sioni Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the cathedral and its surroundings together. Then try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer and make it stand out more against the roofline. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the courtyard if you want to fit in the church and the tower together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Sioni Street (the lane to the south of the church). The cathedral's bell tower framed against the Old Town roofline. Treat the exact spot as approximate and shift a little until the view is clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the phone level so the church and tower do not lean. If you try the lane to the south and the bell tower comes into view, put it on one of the vertical lines, with the rooftops filling the lower part of the frame. As another option, go into the courtyard and use the freestanding bell tower as the focal point for a shot of the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cathedral or the bell tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the pale stone keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands and tuck your elbows in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Going early may help avoid crowds, and soft light early or late in the day tends to flatter the stone.

text.access_note: This is a working Orthodox cathedral, and rules on photographing inside differ and may be restricted during services, so check the official site before you go.

name: National Botanical Garden of Georgia
label: Botanical Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'National Botanical Garden of Georgia' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Green valley behind Narikala with a waterfall.

text.description: This is Tbilisi's big green pocket: a wooded gorge tucked behind Narikala Fortress, with a waterfall running down through it. The photo most visitors come for is taken from the panoramic lookout just left of the main entrance gate. From there you look along the gorge to the waterfall, with the garden's trees framing both sides, and you don't need a long climb to reach it. The garden covers 161 hectares and holds more than 4,500 plant groups, so there is plenty to explore beyond the lookout. Its roots go back centuries. A French traveller, Jean Chardin, described royal gardens on this site in 1671, and it was officially established as a botanical garden in 1845. In 2018 it gained new walking and cycling lanes, which makes wandering with a phone in hand easy. For the best result, take one wide shot from the lookout, then move in closer on details such as the water, leaves and stonework. Keep the waterfall in the middle distance and let the trees make a natural frame around it. If you have time, the view down into the garden from Narikala Fortress shows the wooded valley with the Old Town roofs beyond, and there is another view of the garden from behind the Mother of Georgia statue above it.
text.geographic_location: In the Tsavkisis-Tskali Gorge on the southern foothills of the Sololaki Range, in the heart of Tbilisi. The main entrance sits at the foot of Narikala Fortress, just above the Old Town.
text.directions_text: Start from the Old Town and head for Narikala Fortress; the garden's main entrance is at the foot of the fortress hill. By taxi or hired scooter, ask for the National Botanical Garden's main entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole gorge, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the waterfall itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here your photo shows a wide view of the gorge and the waterfall running through it, framed by the garden's trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the waterfall on one of the vertical lines, with branches or treetops across the top corners as a frame. Keep the horizon level. For a different angle, try the view from Narikala Fortress, looking down over the wooded valley.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the waterfall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright water and sky keep their detail. If the gorge is wide and shaded, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives the softest light. The gorge goes into shadow early, so don't leave your main photos until just before closing time.

text.access_note: The garden is a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go for current ticket rules and opening times.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning and late afternoon give the softest light at the garden (from guides).
The gorge falls into shadow early in the day.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) suits a wide gorge view and gridlines help keep the horizon level.
The Old Town is close to the garden's main entrance.

name: Georgian National Opera Theater
label: Opera and Ballet
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rustaveli Avenue' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Rustaveli Avenue nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/59151604: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tbilisi Opera and Ballet State Theatre' (120 m across).
notes: Moorish-style opera house on Rustaveli Avenue.

text.description:
The Tbilisi Opera and Ballet Theatre, also called the Paliashvili Theatre, is the main opera house of Georgia and sits on Rustaveli Avenue. The company was founded in 1851, and since 1896 it has lived in the present Neo-Moorish building, designed by the architect Victor Schröter. The front is the part to photograph: horseshoe arches, striped stonework and turrets, with the stone buildings along the avenue around it. Inside, the layout is that of a typical European opera house, so the Oriental look is all in the decoration. The theatre was damaged by several fires over the years, and the most recent restoration finished in January 2016 after six years of work.

It photographs well from the pavement across the avenue, where you can fit the whole front into one frame. The facade is said to stand out most after dark, when it is lit, so an evening visit is worth planning. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the arches and the vertical lines of the turrets stay straight. If you arrive along the tree-lined avenue, you will also get a pleasant view of the building coming into sight. Photography inside is a separate matter, so check the official site before you go if you hope to take pictures there.
text.geographic_location: In Tbilisi, on Rustaveli Avenue. The theatre's Neo-Moorish front faces the avenue.
text.directions_text: Once you reach the avenue, cross to the pavement opposite the main front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the avenue. If the whole front will not fit, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the phone level so the building does not lean. Use 2x only for details such as the arches and stripes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rustaveli Avenue (on the pavement across the avenue from the main facade). The full Neo-Moorish front with its horseshoe arches, striped stonework and turrets, framed against the stone buildings along the avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up so its vertical edges follow them. Include a little of the neighbouring stone buildings to frame the theatre. For a different view, walk back along the avenue to the east, where the facade comes into sight down the tree-lined street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little in the evening so the lit stonework does not burn out. If the light is low, let night mode work and hold the phone still against a wall or post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the facade is lit.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the public pavement on the avenue, but the theatre is a working venue, so check the official site before you go if you want to see or photograph inside.

name: Tbilisi TV Broadcasting Tower
label: Tbilisi TV Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mtatsminda Park' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Mtatsminda Park Map' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/437940450: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tbilisi TV Broadcasting Tower' (94 m across).
notes: Lit-up broadcasting tower on Mtatsminda hill.

text.description:
The Tbilisi TV Broadcasting Tower is a slim, free-standing red-and-white mast that rises above the city from the top of a mountain. It was built in 1972 and replaced an earlier tower from 1955, which was moved to the area near Gori. The tower is 274.5 m high and stands on a mountain 719.2 m above sea level, so it looks tall even before you count the hill under it. That is why it works well in photos: it is a clean vertical shape against the sky, with the city spread out far below.

The best photo area is the park ground south-west of the tower on the Mtatsminda Park plateau. From there you can show the tower rising above the park with the city below. Guides describe these public park areas as the main place to photograph it. For a second option, Beritashvili Street gives you the opposite view: the city in the foreground with the tower on the hill above. You can see the tower from there, with the city below.

You do not need to go inside the tower, and you shouldn't plan on it, because it is unclear whether visitors can enter, so check on the day. Stay in the open park and take your shots from there. Evening is the strongest time, when the tower is lit. Give yourself a few minutes to walk around the park and try more than one angle, since the mast looks quite different when you change distance.
text.geographic_location: The tower stands on a mountain above Tbilisi, in the area of Mtatsminda Park. From the park you look down over the city.
text.directions_text: The tower is about 264 m to the north-east of it, a short walk. The tower is tall, so you will be able to see it as you walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x): from about 264 m away, it helps fit the whole mast and some of the park in the frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of the tower with the city below it. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the top of the tower against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Mtatsminda Park (area around the tower base on the mountain plateau). The red-and-white tower rising above the park with the city spread out below it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the mast up with a vertical line. Tilt the phone only as much as you must, because tilting makes the tower lean inwards. Put some park, trees or paths in the lower part of the frame so the tower has something to rise from. As an alternative, Beritashvili Street shows the city in the foreground with the tower on the hill above it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the tower to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky stays rich and the lit tower doesn't blow out. When the tower is lit in the evening, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall, railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the tower is illuminated.

text.access_note: Photographing from the public areas of Mtatsminda Park is described as unrestricted, but access to the tower itself is unclear, so check locally whether the tower is open.
claims_not_in_sources: From about 264 m away, the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit the whole mast and some of the park in the frame.
Tilting the phone upwards makes vertical lines lean inwards.
Night mode works better if the phone is held steady against a support.

name: Museum of Soviet Occupation (Tbilisi)
label: Soviet Occupation Muse
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.

notes: Part of the Georgian National Museum on Rustaveli Avenue.

text.description: The Museum of the Soviet Occupation sits on Rustaveli Avenue, Tbilisi's main thoroughfare, and is part of the Georgian National Museum. It opened on 26 May 2006, Georgia's Independence Day, and tells the story of the Soviet years in Georgia, from 1921 to 1991. Inside is a permanent exhibition of around 3,000 items, including archive documents, photographs, video and objects from Soviet-era prison cells. It makes a good stop for a phone photo because it stands on the city's main street, so you can pair the building with the busy boulevard around it. Use the street as context: a wide shot shows how the museum fits into the avenue, while a closer frame lets you pick out the entrance and facade details. Stand on the pavement, keep the whole frontage in view and check the edges of the picture so that passers-by or street furniture do not cut into the building. A few steps either way will change the angle and help you avoid parked cars and signs. Photography rules inside a museum can differ from those outside, so look for signs or ask staff before you take pictures in the galleries. Treat the subject with some care: the exhibition remembers victims of political repression, so a calm, respectful photo suits the place better than a posed or playful one.
text.geographic_location: In central Tbilisi, on Rustaveli Avenue, the city's main thoroughfare, where the museum is administered as part of the Georgian National Museum.
text.directions_text: Start from the Rustaveli Avenue area in central Tbilisi and look for the museum along the avenue. If you are coming from further out, go by taxi and ask to be dropped on Rustaveli Avenue near the museum. The phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so once you reach the building you are in the right place. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building from the pavement. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the whole frontage in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the entrance or signage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, step back along the pavement as far as is safe to widen your view of the frontage.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's edges with the vertical lines so it does not lean. Keep the museum filling most of the frame, with a little of Rustaveli Avenue around it to show where it is. Take a second, closer shot of the entrance for detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the facade is not washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is easiest for clear photos of the exterior. Earlier in the day the pavements are usually quieter, which makes it easier to get a clean frame. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The museum is part of the Georgian National Museum, so check the official site before you go for opening times, entry rules and photography rules inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Pavements along Rustaveli Avenue can be busy with passers-by, and earlier in the day they are usually quieter.
Photography rules inside museum galleries can differ from those outside.
The pavement in front of the museum may be narrow enough that ultra-wide helps.

name: Juma Mosque, Tbilisi
label: Juma Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Botanikuri Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Botanikuri Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/506741615: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Juma Mosque' (47 m across).
notes: Old town mosque near the sulfur baths.

text.description:
The Juma Mosque is the only mosque still standing in Tbilisi's historic Old Town, and it is a good subject for a phone. The walls are red brick with arched windows, and a tall octagonal minaret rises above them. The building mixes Neo-Gothic and Islamic details, and colourful mosaics decorate both the outside and the inside. It sits at the foot of Narikala Fortress, so the steep slope and cliff behind it give your photo a dramatic backdrop.

The site has been a mosque for a long time. An early 18th-century Ottoman mosque was destroyed in the 1740s, and a rebuild followed in 1846-1851. The current red-brick building dates from 1895 and was restored in 1998. Sunni and Shia Muslims pray together here, which is unusual.

The quietest and most rewarding approach is to walk uphill along Botanikuri Street from the sulphur baths. The mosque appears at the top of the street, with the minaret clear against the slope. Take your main photo here, then step in closer for detail shots of the brickwork and mosaics. If you have time, Chreli Abano gives a view of the tiled bathhouse front with the minaret behind, and Narikala Fortress looks down over the mosque and the bath domes (check the fortress access details before you go). Keep the exterior as your focus, and ask permission before photographing worshippers or going inside.
text.geographic_location: In the Abanotubani (sulphur baths) area of Tbilisi's Old Town, at the upper end of Botanikuri Street. It stands at the foot of Narikala Fortress, among the bathhouses.
text.directions_text: Go to the Abanotubani sulphur baths area in the Old Town. From the baths, walk uphill along Botanikuri Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the mosque, the minaret and the slope behind in one frame. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the minaret top, the arched windows and the mosaics. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer and want the whole facade, and keep the phone level so the walls do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Botanikuri Street (walking uphill from the sulfur baths; the mosque sits at the upper end of the street). The red-brick mosque and its tall octagonal minaret seen straight on along the street, with the steep slope and cliff setting behind it. The mosque is just to the south-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the minaret on one of the vertical lines, with the street leading the eye up to the building. Include a little of the slope behind to show how the mosque sits against the cliff. For a different view, Chreli Abano shows the tiled bathhouse front with the minaret rising behind, and Narikala Fortress looks down on the mosque and the bath domes.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out and the red brick keeps its colour. Turn on gridlines to keep the vertical lines of the minaret straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the brick and mosaics.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so photograph the exterior from the street, dress modestly if you go in, and ask permission before photographing inside or any worshippers.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters brick and mosaics.
Modest dress is usually expected when visiting a mosque.

name: Kashveti Church
label: Kashveti Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '9 აპრილის პარკი' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '9 აპრილის სახელობის ბაღი' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/65299828: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kashveti Church of St. George' (45 m across).

text.description:
Kashveti Church of St. George is a Georgian Orthodox church in central Tbilisi, standing across Rustaveli Avenue from the Parliament building. It was built between 1904 and 1910 by the architect Leopold Bilfeldt, who took the medieval Samtavisi Cathedral as his model. It replaced an older brick church put up in 1753 at the request of the Amilakhvari family. The frescoes inside were painted by Lado Gudiashvili in 1947. The name comes from Georgian words for 'stone' and 'to give birth', linked to a legend about the monk David of Gareja.

Most visitors photograph the church from the busy avenue in front. This spot suggests something calmer: the park called 9 აპრილის პარკი, directly behind the church. From there you get a quieter, more distant view of the church's rear and its dome, without the traffic and pavement crowds. It is a good place to try a tighter, more restful picture of the stonework and dome against the sky.

The park is not a classic viewpoint, so walk around a little and check the framing on site. If you also want the pale stone facade and arched entrance, with the dome and bell tower and the Parliament building opposite, you can take that from the avenue side. Keep the pavement clear for other people, and photograph the exterior only unless photography is clearly allowed inside.
text.geographic_location: Kashveti Church is in central Tbilisi on Rustaveli Avenue, directly opposite the Parliament building. The park behind the church, 9 აპრილის პარკი, is the viewpoint nearby.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground or tram stops listed for this spot, so walk or navigate to Kashveti Church on Rustaveli Avenue in central Tbilisi, opposite the Parliament building. The park, 9 აპრილის პარკი, is the viewpoint nearby, so check on site where the park edge falls. Keep the church to your south-west as you settle into the view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to pick out the rear of the church and its dome from behind. Use the default lens (1x) for a wider picture that includes trees and the park around the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 9 აპრილის პარკი (directly behind the church). A quieter, more distant view back toward the church's rear and dome from the park grounds behind it. The pale stone facade and arched entrance are on the avenue side, so you will not see them from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the dome up on a vertical line, keeping the walls straight. Use trees or the park path as a natural frame at the edge of the picture. If you want the facade with the bell tower and the Parliament building opposite, walk round to Rustaveli Avenue, but stay off the busy pavement edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out the pale stone. Hold the phone with both hands, and keep Live Photos off unless you want movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning light is usually kinder to the stonework, but the best direction can vary, so check how the light falls when you arrive.

text.access_note: The church is an active place of worship, so be quiet and respectful, use no flash, and ask before photographing inside; check the official site before you go for any visiting rules.

text.description:
Surb Nshan, also called the Church of the Holy Seal, is an Armenian church in Old Tbilisi. It was built between 1703 and 1711 and reconstructed in 1780, so it is more than three centuries old. It was partially destroyed by arson in 2002 and still looks dilapidated. That is part of why it makes an honest, atmospheric photo: weathered walls and a building that clearly has a long story. Please photograph it as you find it and don't expect a polished monument.

Start with a wide frame that shows the whole building and the ground around it. Then step in and look for details: stonework, doorways, the shape of the roofline and the texture of damaged areas. Keep the gridlines on so the walls and roof stay straight, and tilt the phone slightly upwards only if you are happy with some converging lines. If people walk through the scene, wait a moment or take a few frames, as a person can show the scale of the building. Because the church is in a damaged state, it is wise to stay on open public ground and keep to any barriers or signs.
text.geographic_location: Surb Nshan Church is in Old Tbilisi, in the historic part of the city. It is an Armenian church of the early 18th century.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so use the map to reach Old Tbilisi and then the phone icon on the map. From there the church is about 32 metres to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. If the church is not in sight, follow the map towards the church rather than guessing at side streets. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are squeezed for space and want the whole building in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for stonework and roof details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Take one wide shot to show the whole church, then a closer one of a door, window or damaged wall. Turn on the gridlines and line up the walls with them. Take a second version with a little foreground, such as a path or a wall, to add depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its colour and texture. Take a few frames in case of passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight, in the morning or late afternoon, usually shows stone texture best. Harsh midday sun can flatten the walls and darken the damaged areas.

text.access_note: This is a church that is damaged and may be closed or fenced off, so check local information before you go, and stay on open public ground.
